name: Matrix multiplication 4,4,4
description: Find a rank-minimal exact tensor decomposition for multiplying a 4 by 4 matrix by a 4 by 4 matrix. The output factor follows the official trace convention W[k*n+i,r].

requirements.hardware: CPU
requirements.datasets: Exact mathematical identity; no dataset required.

notes: Paper Appendix A reports exact integer/half-integer decompositions. The reimplementation checks every tensor coefficient with exact integer arithmetic.
The naive rank n*m*p baseline validates the evaluator; it does not reproduce the paper search or reported rank.
Published decomposition verified with the unmodified official notebook function and the independent exact integer evaluator.
execution.interface: solve(instance) -> {U,V,W}, column factors in trace order; see docs/INTERFACE.md

limitations: Independent exact task evaluator derived from Appendix A; does not reproduce AlphaEvolve search or its learned constructions.
Coefficient domain matches reported integer/half-integer (or Gaussian half-integer) representation; it is not unrestricted tensor rank over every scalar field.

U shape (n*m,rank), V shape (m*p,rank), W shape (p*n,rank)
Half-integer real coefficients; only the three explicitly documented complex shapes permit half-integer real and imaginary parts

task_setup_instructions: poetry install
notes: This task selects the frozen paper reproduction archive at Zenodo 14917719. The later GitHub implementation is retained only as a source reference.

The paper Zenodo archive was downloaded, its published MD5 verified, and source inspected. It provides the exact run_BP_HPO.py script and frozen library; see archive_execution. Commands run in the extracted paper archive; the current GitHub checkout is a separate, later implementation.

Archive README specifies Poetry1.7.1+ and Python3.10. Run poetry install, configure OPENAI_API_KEY, then poetry run python run_BP_HPO.py. Default model is gpt-4o-2024-05-13; verify availability before running.
The archived full search incurs API calls and substantial SMAC/benchmark compute. It creates experiment logs/results; paper result plotting is also available as plot_BP.py.
Source is pinned by the archive SHA256. Archived scripts start the full experiment immediately when invoked; use the command preview to inspect settings before executing.

Archived BP raw evaluator returns (mean bins used - mean L1 lower bound) / mean L1 lower bound: a dimensionless excess fraction to minimize, with no multiplication by 100. run_BP_HPO.py negates this value for maximization.
Paper Section4.1 instead defines mean_i(lb_i / n_i), a ratio to maximize. This differs from the archived score in formula and scale; both definitions are preserved separately.

task_setup_instructions: poetry install
notes: This task selects the frozen paper reproduction archive at Zenodo 14917719. The later GitHub implementation is retained only as a source reference.

The paper Zenodo archive was downloaded, its published MD5 verified, and source inspected. It provides the exact run_TSP_HPO.py script and frozen library; see archive_execution. Commands run in the extracted paper archive; the current GitHub checkout is a separate, later implementation.

Archive README specifies Poetry1.7.1+ and Python3.10. Run poetry install, configure OPENAI_API_KEY, then poetry run python run_TSP_HPO.py. Default model is gpt-4o-2024-05-13; verify availability before running.
The archived full search incurs API calls and substantial SMAC/benchmark compute. It creates experiment logs/results; paper result plotting is also available as plot_TSP.py.
Source is pinned by the archive SHA256. Archived scripts start the full experiment immediately when invoked; use the command preview to inspect settings before executing.

Archived TSP raw evaluator computes 100 * (best tour length / optimum length - 1) for each instance and averages the 64 values; units are percent and lower is better. run_TSP_HPO.py negates this mean for maximization.
Each archived search instance allows 10 seconds and 1000 GLS iterations; final paper evaluation uses separate larger test suites.

notes: Paper-guided reconstruction, not the original FunBO implementation or a paper-result reproduction. No dedicated official FunBO source repository was verified.
AppendixC.1 Table1 domains, grid cardinalities, fixed zero-mean RBF GP lengthscales/variance/noise are preserved; one initial worst grid point and30 acquisition decisions follow Figures8/9.

Original grid/seed not published in inspected sources: scipy.stats.qmc.Sobol(scramble=True,seed=0) creates a fixed dyadic sequence, truncated to the exact paper grid size. The returned grid and objective SHA256 values identify it.

Reported score is normalized simple regret relative to the same discrete grid optimum; raw regret and trials-to-grid-optimum are retained. It is not error relative to an unknown continuous optimum or the two-term FunSearch training reward.

GP prediction is implemented with SciPy Cholesky, including Gaussian likelihood variance as in GPy.predict; bounded numerical jitter, if needed, is reported. Candidate returns a validated integer index from predictive mean/variance arrays and incumbent.
The seed is expected improvement with the paper Figure8 interface; no discovered FunBO AF or MetaBO policy result is claimed.

name: Santa 2025: Christmas tree packing (n = 1..200)
description: For every n from 1 to 200 place n copies of the competition's fixed 15-vertex tree polygon (rotations allowed, no overlaps, coordinates within [-100, 100]) so that the bounding square of each configuration is as small as possible; the score is the sum over n of (bounding-square area / n), lower is better.

sources.locator: Competition overview and evaluation page (task statement, metric definition, submission format)
Getting-started notebook (tree geometry, collision rule, greedy sample submission)

requirements.hardware: CPU
requirements.datasets: None: the tree polygon is fixed and every configuration is constructed by the candidate.

evaluation.benchmark: Kaggle Santa 2025 - Christmas Tree Packing Challenge
evaluation.paper_metric: sum over n of bounding-square area / n

execution.interface: construct(n) -> array of shape (n, 3): rows (x, y, deg) for the n-tree configuration; called for every n in 1..200

limitations: The evaluator is an independent reimplementation of the competition metric (same polygon, scaling factor, overlap rule and bounding-square formula) and reproduces the official code's doctest value and the sample submission's score exactly; it is not the Kaggle scoring service.
No leaderboard value is embedded; the reference value is the getting-started sample submission (176.60550959158516).

arithmetic_kakeya_distribution.docstring:
Arithmetic Kakeya conjecture (entropy formulation). Construct a joint probability
distribution P[y, x] of two discrete random variables X, Y supported on an n x n grid
(here n = 10) so as to maximize the entropy projection ratio

    H(pi_{r_inf}) / max_i H(pi_{r_i}),

where pi_r(x, y) = x + r * y projects the grid along slope r, H is the Shannon entropy
(in bits) of the resulting projected distribution, the finite slopes are
r_1, ..., r_k = 0.0, 1.0, 2.0 and the distinguished slope is r_inf = -1.0.

The baseline is the uniform distribution over the grid.

Returns:
    P: np.ndarray of shape (10, 10), non-negative and summing to 1, where P[y, x] is the
        joint probability that X = x and Y = y.

beat_the_average_measure.docstring:
Beat-the-average game. Construct a discrete probability measure mu on [0, inf)
that maximizes P[X1 + X2 + X3 < 2*X4], where X1, X2, X3, X4 are i.i.d. with law mu.
The goal is to push the achievable lower bound on the constant
C = sup_mu P[X1 + X2 + X3 < 2*X4] as high as possible.

Baseline (from the upstream notebook): the uniform measure on {0, 1, ..., n-1}.
Here n = 32.

Returns:
    support: np.ndarray of shape (n,), non-negative support points of the measure.
    weights: np.ndarray of shape (n,), non-negative weights (need not be normalized;
        the evaluator normalizes them to sum to 1).

block_stacking30.docstring:
Block-stacking (single-wide overhang) problem. Stack n identical rigid blocks of
width 1 at the edge of a table (table edge at x = 0). Let x_k be the horizontal
position of block k (its center), with 0 = x_0 <= x_1 <= ... <= x_n. Maximize the
horizontal displacement x_n of the top (n-th) block over the table edge subject to
the stack remaining stable, i.e. for every 0 <= i < n the center of mass of all
blocks above block i must lie within block i's footprint (and the whole stack's
center of mass must lie over the table). Here n = 30.

Baseline construction: the classical harmonic ("1/2, 1/4, 1/6, ...") staircase,
which achieves the known optimum C(n) = (1/2) * H_n, where H_n is the n-th harmonic
number. Block k is offset so that x_k = (1/2)(H_n - H_{n-k-1}).

Returns:
    positions: np.ndarray of shape (30,) with the horizontal center positions
        x_1, ..., x_n of the blocks, non-decreasing and positive.

hausdorff_young_p32.docstring:
Hausdorff-Young inequality, probing the Babenko-Beckner constant.

Construct a bounded, integrable, not-identically-zero step function f of one real
variable that maximizes the quotient

    Q(f) = ||fhat||_q / ||f||_p ,     with 1/p + 1/q = 1, p = 3/2, q = 3,

where fhat is the Fourier transform fhat(xi) = integral f(x) exp(-2*pi*i*x*xi) dx.

The function is represented as a step function on the interval [-R, R]: cell j
(j = 0 .. N-1) spans [x_j, x_j + dx) with x_j = -R + j*dx and dx = 2R/N, and f takes
the constant value returned in entry j of the array. The sharp maximizer of the
Hausdorff-Young ratio is a Gaussian (Babenko-Beckner), so the baseline samples the
Gaussian exp(-x^2) on the grid.

Returns:
    values: np.ndarray of shape (N,), the step-function value of f on each grid cell.

crouzeix_conjecture4.docstring:
Crouzeix's conjecture probe. Find a complex n x n matrix A and a polynomial p
(given by its complex coefficients, highest degree first, as in numpy.poly1d)
that make the Crouzeix ratio

    R(A, p) = || p(A) ||_op  /  sup_{z in W(A)} |p(z)|

as large as possible, where || . ||_op is the spectral (operator) norm and

    W(A) = { <A x, x> : ||x|| <= 1 }

is the numerical range (field of values) of A. Crouzeix's conjecture states
that R(A, p) <= 2 for every A and p; the bound 2 is approached by the
construction below. Here the size is baked to n = 4.

The baseline is the AlphaEvolve "optimal" tridiagonal construction: a
nilpotent matrix with sqrt(2) on the first and last super-diagonal entries
and 1 on the interior super-diagonal entries, paired with p(z) = z^(n-1).

Returns:
    A: np.ndarray of shape (4, 4), complex dtype, the matrix.
    poly_coeffs: np.ndarray of shape (4,), the polynomial coefficients in
        descending-degree order (numpy.poly1d convention). Here this encodes
        p(z) = z^3.

erdos_discrepancy_pattern.docstring:
Erdos discrepancy problem. Build the longest possible sign pattern
a_1, ..., a_N in {-1, +1} whose discrepancy is at most 2, where the
discrepancy is the maximum value of |a_d + a_{2d} + ... + a_{kd}| taken over
all homogeneous progressions d, 2d, ..., kd contained in {1, ..., N}.

This baseline uses a deterministic greedy construction: it appends signs one
at a time, at each step choosing the sign (+1 or -1) that keeps every
homogeneous-progression partial sum within [-2, 2], breaking ties by
minimizing the sum of squared partial sums. It stops as soon as neither sign
can be appended without exceeding discrepancy 2.

Returns:
    pattern: np.ndarray of shape (N,) and integer dtype, with every entry
        equal to +1 or -1. N is determined by how far the greedy
        construction can extend while keeping discrepancy <= 2.

erdos_gyarfas_graph.docstring:
Erdős-Gyárfás counterexample search. Construct a finite simple graph G whose
minimum degree is at least 3, trying to AVOID any cycle whose length is a power
of two (4, 8, 16, ...). The Erdős-Gyárfás conjecture states no such graph exists;
we search for a counterexample (or, failing that, a graph with as few power-of-two

erdos_squarefree500.docstring:
Erdos squarefree problem. For N = 500, find a subset A of {1, ..., N} of maximum
size such that a*b + 1 is NOT square-free for every pair a, b in A (a square-free
integer is one not divisible by any perfect square > 1). Larger feasible subsets
are better; pairs whose a*b + 1 is square-free are penalized as violations.

Baseline construction: the residue class 7 (mod 25). If a, b == 7 (mod 25) then
a*b == 49 == -1 (mod 25), so a*b + 1 == 0 (mod 25) is divisible by 5^2 and is never
square-free. This yields zero violations for any pair drawn from the class.

Returns:
    subset: 1-D np.ndarray of distinct integers in {1, ..., 500} forming the subset A.

factoring_factorials100.docstring:
Factoring N! into N factors (here N = 100). Let A034258-style C(N) be the largest
quantity such that N! can be written as a product of exactly N integer factors that are
all >= C(N). Equivalently, partition the multiset of prime factors of N! into N groups
(bins) and maximize the minimum group product. The objective is to make the smallest of
the N factors as large as possible.

Solution representation (numpy-array form required by this template):
    The prime factors of N! are enumerated in a fixed canonical order: the sorted-ascending
    list of all prime factors of N! counted with multiplicity, e.g. [2, 2, ..., 3, 3, ...,
    5, ...]. This constructor returns a 1-D integer assignment array `assign` of that same
    length, where assign[i] in {0, ..., N-1} is the bin (factor) that the i-th canonical
    prime factor is placed into. The N factor values are then the products of the primes in
    each bin, and the score is the minimum of those N products.

Baseline construction:
    A multiplicative longest-processing-time greedy: sort the prime factors descending and
    repeatedly assign the next largest prime to the bin that currently has the smallest
    product (balancing the bins). Deterministic.

Returns:
    assign: np.ndarray of shape (Omega(N!),) and integer dtype, with values in [0, N-1],
        giving the bin index of each canonical prime factor. For N = 100 the length is 239.

nikodym_set.docstring:
Construct a Nikodym set in F_q^2 with q = p^2 and p = 7. A set N is a Nikodym
set if, for every point x in F_q^2, there exists a direction v != 0 such that
the punctured line {x + t*v : t in F_q, t != 0} is fully contained in N. The
goal is to make N as SMALL as possible, equivalently to make its complement
(the excluded set) as LARGE as possible.

Field model: F_q is built as F_p[alpha] with alpha^2 = k, where k is the
smallest quadratic non-residue mod p. An element of F_q is the pair (a, b)
standing for a + b*alpha, with a, b in {0, ..., p-1}.

Baseline construction (the "skip step 2.5" construction from the AlphaEvolve
notebook, of size p^4 - p^2*(p+1)/2): take the Hermitian unital
    U = {(x, y) : Trace(x) + Norm(y) = 0},  with Trace((a,b)) = 2a,
    Norm((a,b)) = a^2 - b^2*k.
Build the blocking set B = points of U whose y-coordinate lies in the special
set Y = {(u^2 mod p, v) : u, v in F_p}. The excluded set is S = U \ B, and the
Nikodym set is everything else: N = (F_q^2) \ S.

Returns:
    points: np.ndarray of shape (k, 2, 2) integer array. Each of the k points
    is [[x_a, x_b], [y_a, y_b]] with the F_q coordinates x = (x_a, x_b) and
    y = (y_a, y_b), all entries in [0, p).

Construct a binary sequence a of length N = 41 with entries in {-1, +1} that maximizes the

function_guessing_game_strategy.docstring:
Offline proxy for AlphaEvolve Problem 66 ("The function guessing game").

In the original (interactive) problem, an agent must guess a hidden function
f: R -> R, paying 1 currency unit per evaluation f(x), and earning a reward of
1000 currency units if it reconstructs the function accurately (L^1 error below a
small threshold). The deterministic, offline core of that game is: decide AT WHICH
POINTS to evaluate the hidden function so that, given only those samples, the
function can be reconstructed exactly while paying as little as possible.

A guessing strategy is therefore a fixed set of query locations x_1, ..., x_k in the
domain [-1, 1]. The evaluator probes each hidden test function at these locations,
reconstructs it by polynomial (least-squares) interpolation, and scores the strategy
by the net reward = 1000 * (fraction reconstructed correctly) - k, i.e. reward minus
the per-evaluation query cost.

A polynomial of degree D is uniquely determined by D + 1 distinct samples, so the
optimal strategy queries exactly D + 1 well-placed points. This baseline plays it
safe with 12 equally-spaced query points: it reconstructs every degree-5 test
function exactly, but overpays on queries, leaving headroom for evolution to reduce
the number of queries toward the optimum of 6.

Returns:
    query_points: np.ndarray of shape (k,) giving the x-locations (in [-1, 1]) at
        which the hidden function will be evaluated.

furstenberg_sarkozy_205.docstring:
Furstenberg-Sarkozy problem (modular formulation). Find a subset of Z/mZ of maximum
size that does NOT contain any two elements differing by a nonzero perfect k-th power
modulo m. Here m = 205 and k = 2 (squares), i.e. forbidden differences are the nonzero
quadratic residues modulo 205.

The returned subset is the AlphaEvolve search target: the larger it is (while staying
feasible) the better. The AlphaEvolve record for this instance is a subset of size 12.

The notebook's literal search seed is the trivial subset [0]; here we use a slightly
stronger but still simple deterministic greedy construction as the starting point so
evolution has something concrete to improve on.

Returns:
    subset: np.ndarray of shape (s,), dtype int, a list of distinct residues in
        {0, ..., 204} with no two differing by a nonzero square modulo 205.

grid_tiling_imo2025_p6_n36.docstring:
IMO 2025 Problem 6 (grid tiling). On an n x n grid of unit squares, place
non-overlapping axis-aligned rectangular tiles (sides on grid lines) so that
every row and every column has exactly one uncovered unit square. Minimize the
number of tiles. Here n = 36 (optimal tile count is n + 2*sqrt(n) - 3 = 45).

Baseline construction: leave the main diagonal uncovered (one uncovered cell
per row and per column), then greedily cover the rest with maximal rectangles
(extend right, then down). This is a valid but non-optimal tiling, so there is
plenty of room to improve toward the optimum.

Returns:
    tiles: np.ndarray of shape (T, 4) with integer rows (r0, c0, r1, c1). Each
        tile covers grid rows r0 <= r < r1 and columns c0 <= c < c1 (top-left
        corner inclusive, bottom-right corner exclusive).

kakeya_needle_2d_positions64.docstring:
Two-dimensional Kakeya-needle area-minimization problem. For a fixed n, choose
base positions x = (x_0, ..., x_{n-1}). For position index i (0-based) let
a_i = (i + 1) / n and define the triangle R_i with vertices
    (x_i, 0), (x_i + 1/n, 0), (x_i + a_i, 1).
Every triangle has base width 1/n on the line y = 0 and its apex on the line
y = 1. The objective is to choose x so that the AREA of the union of the n
triangles R_i is as small as possible. Here n = 64.

This baseline uses the classical Keich construction (valid for n a power of 2):
expand a_i = i/n in binary as a_i = sum_j eps_j 2^{-j} and set
    x_i = sum_{j=1}^{k} ((1 - j) / k) * eps_j * 2^{-j},   k = log2(n).

Returns:
    positions: np.ndarray of shape (64,) with the base x-coordinates x_i.

kakeya_needle_3d8.docstring:
Three-dimensional discrete Kakeya needle problem with grid parameter N = 8.

We build N*N = 64 "generalized tubes" indexed by (i, j), i, j in {0, ..., N-1}.
Tube (i, j) has a base position (x, y) and, at height c in [0, 1], occupies the
axis-aligned square
    [x + c*i/N, x + 1/N + c*i/N] x [y + c*j/N, y + 1/N + c*j/N].
So the tube is a unit-height prism of square cross-section 1/N x 1/N that is
sheared so its top face is offset by (i/N, j/N): the (i, j) pair selects the
needle direction, and all N*N directions are covered. The task is to choose the
64 base positions so that the VOLUME of the union of all tubes is as SMALL as
possible (a Kakeya/Besicovitch-type set: needles in every direction, tiny measure).

Because the (i, j) grid is a full product and each square is a product of an
x-interval (a function of i) and a y-interval (a function of j), placing the base
x only as a function of i and the base y only as a function of j makes the union a
product of two 1-D unions. This baseline uses the Keich binary construction
(the 2-D Kakeya analogue, here for N = 2^k = 8) independently in x and y.

Returns:
    positions: np.ndarray of shape (64, 2). Row k = tube k in (i, j) raster order
        (i outer, j inner, i.e. numpy meshgrid indexing="ij" then flatten),
        column 0 = base x-coordinate, column 1 = base y-coordinate.

kissing_cylinders7.docstring:
Arrange n mutually tangent infinite unit-radius cylinders in R^3 (the "kissing
cylinders" problem). Each cylinder is described by its axis line: a point P on the
axis and a unit direction vector v. Two unit cylinders are tangent (kiss) when the
shortest distance between their axis lines equals 2 (the sum of the two radii). The
objective is to make every pair of cylinders mutually tangent. Here n = 7.

Returns:
    cylinders: np.ndarray of shape (7, 2, 3). For cylinder i, cylinders[i, 0] is the
        point P on its axis (taken closest to the origin, i.e. P . v = 0) and
        cylinders[i, 1] is the unit direction vector v of its axis.

moving_sofa_2d.docstring:
The 2D moving-sofa problem: find the largest-area rigid shape that can be moved
through an L-shaped corridor of width 1 that makes a single 90-degree turn.

The shape is specified IMPLICITLY by a motion "path". Each path point is a triple
(x, y, angle_degrees) giving the position of the corridor's inner corner and the
corridor's rotation at one instant of the move. In the reference frame of the sofa
the corridor sweeps over the plane; the sofa is then the intersection of every
corridor placement along the path, so by construction it always clears the corridor.
The objective is to maximize the area of that intersection.

The evaluator prepends the start state (0, 0, 0) and appends the end state
(-2, 0, 90), then densifies the path to <=1-degree rotation steps, exactly as in the
AlphaEvolve "single turn" corridor notebook.

Returns:
    path: np.ndarray of shape (n, 3); each row is (x, y, angle_degrees) for the
        corridor's inner corner. Here n = 8. Endpoints are added by the evaluator.

moving_sofa_3d_path.docstring:
The 3D moving sofa problem: find the largest-volume rigid 3D shape that can
travel through an L-shaped 3D corridor of unit cross-section that has two
90-degree turns - one in the X-Y plane and one in the Y-Z plane (a 3D
generalisation of the classical 2D moving sofa problem).

The shape itself is recovered (in the evaluator) by sweeping a solid block
along a motion path and keeping every sub-volume that stays inside the
corridor for the whole path. The "solution" we evolve is therefore that
motion path: a sequence of rigid-body poses for the block.

A pose is a 6-tuple (x, y, z, yaw, pitch, roll), where (yaw, pitch, roll)
are extrinsic Euler angles in DEGREES (applied about the fixed z, y, x axes,
i.e. R = Rx(roll) @ Ry(pitch) @ Rz(yaw)) and (x, y, z) is a translation. To
place the block in a pose we first rotate it about the origin, then
translate it. The evaluator prepends a fixed start pose and appends a fixed
end pose, then densifies (smooths) the path before sweeping the block.

This baseline path is exactly the construction AlphaEvolve reported for this
problem in "Mathematical Discovery and Exploration at Scale" (2025), which
achieves a swept volume of about 1.81 at fine grid resolution.

Returns:
    path: np.ndarray of shape (99, 6), each row a pose
        (x, y, z, yaw_deg, pitch_deg, roll_deg).

no_5_on_a_sphere8.docstring:
The "no 5 on a sphere" problem. Select as many points as possible from the
n x n x n integer grid {0,...,n-1}^3 such that no five of the selected points
are co-spherical (lie on a common sphere, which also forbids five co-planar
points). Five points p_i = (x_i, y_i, z_i) are co-spherical iff the 5x5
determinant of rows [x_i, y_i, z_i, x_i^2 + y_i^2 + z_i^2, 1] vanishes.

Here n = 8. The objective is to MAXIMIZE the number of selected points.

Baseline construction (mirrors the notebook's randomized greedy search,
translated to pure numpy): run a fixed number of seeded random-order greedy
passes over the grid, adding a point whenever it keeps the set sphere-free,
and keep the largest set found. Deterministic via np.random.seed(0).

Returns:
    points: np.ndarray of shape (k, 3) of integer grid coordinates in
        [0, n-1], no five of which are co-spherical.

ovals_problem20.docstring:
The Ovals problem. For a fixed n, propose three real 1D arrays x, y and phi
(each of length n, viewed as samples at the equally spaced parameters
t_k = 2*pi*k/n, k = 0..n-1). Interpolating these periodically yields smooth
periodic functions f, g, h on [0, 2*pi]. Consider the planar curve
t -> (f(t), g(t)), reparametrized by arc-length s, with curvature kappa(s).
The objective is the Rayleigh quotient

    I(f, g, h) = integral_0^{2*pi} [ h'(s)^2 + (kappa(s) * h(s))^2 ] ds
                 / integral_0^{2*pi} h(s)^2 ds

which must be made AS SMALL AS POSSIBLE, subject to the curve being convex
(the signed curvature must stay strictly positive everywhere). Here n = 20.

Baseline construction: the unit circle with a constant weight, i.e.
x_k = cos(t_k), y_k = sin(t_k), phi_k = 1. For the circle the arc-length
curvature is identically 1 and h is constant, so I = 1 exactly.

Returns:
    (x, y, phi): a tuple of three np.ndarray each of shape (20,) giving the
        sampled values of the x-coordinate, y-coordinate and weight function.

prime_number_theorem_partial_function.docstring:
Construct a partial function f from a subset of the positive integers to the reals
that maximizes a hidden number-theoretic objective related to the Prime Number Theorem.

The function f is scored by a fixed evaluator (see evaluator.py) that:
  * subtracts a constant from f(1) so that sum_k f(k)/k == 0,
  * requires the step function M(x) = sum_k f(k) * floor(x/k) to stay <= 1 for every
    real x in [1, 10*max_key] (otherwise the construction is infeasible), and
  * returns the objective a = -sum_k f(k) * log(k) / k (to be maximized; optimum 1.0).
The optimum is approached by the Mobius function mu(k), for which the classic identity
sum_{k<=x} mu(k) floor(x/k) = 1 holds and -sum mu(k) log(k)/k -> 1.

Representation:
    domain : np.ndarray, shape (m,), dtype int   -> positive integers in the domain of f
    values : np.ndarray, shape (m,), dtype float -> the corresponding real values f(k)

Returns:
    (domain, values): a tuple of two numpy arrays of equal length describing f.

rudin_problem10.docstring:
Rudin problem for polynomials on the 2-sphere. Find the real coefficients
(c_m) for m = -k..k of a real degree-k spherical harmonic

    f = sum_{m=-k}^{k} c_m Y_k^m

on the round unit sphere S^2 that MINIMIZE the norm ratio

    ||f||_{L^4(S^2)} / ||f||_{L^2(S^2)}

(norms taken with the standard surface measure dOmega of total mass 4*pi).
Here the degree is fixed to k = 10, so the returned vector has length
2*k + 1 = 21.

This baseline returns the all-ones coefficient vector (the same simple,
non-degenerate construction used in the upstream notebook's verification
cell); evolution should reshape these coefficients to flatten |f| and drive
the L^4/L^2 ratio down.

Returns:
    coeffs: np.ndarray of shape (21,) with the real coefficients
        c_m, ordered m = -10, -9, ..., 0, ..., 9, 10.

sendov_polynomial6.docstring:
Sendov's conjecture (probing the Sendov bound). For a complex polynomial f of degree n
with all zeros z_1,...,z_n in the closed unit disk, let w_1,...,w_{n-1} be its critical
points (the zeros of f'). The objective is to choose the n roots so as to maximize

    max_{1<=k<=n}  min_{1<=j<=n-1}  |z_k - w_j|

i.e. push some root as far as possible from every critical point. Sendov conjectured
this quantity never exceeds 1; the n-th roots of unity attain exactly 1. Here n = 6.

Returns:
    roots: np.ndarray of shape (6,), complex dtype, with every root inside the closed
        unit disk (|z_k| <= 1).

sidorenko_graphon.docstring:
Sidorenko's conjecture for the bipartite graph H = K_{5,5} minus a perfect
matching (10 vertices, 20 edges, 4-regular bipartite). A graphon is a symmetric
measurable function W: [0,1]^2 -> [0,1]; here it is represented as a step graphon,
i.e. a symmetric n x n matrix M with entries in [0,1] whose value on block (i,j)
equals M[i, j] (the unit square is split into n equal intervals).

Sidorenko's conjecture states that for every graphon W,
    t(H, W) >= t(K2, W)^|E(H)|,
i.e. the ratio  t(H, W) / t(K2, W)^|E(H)|  is at least 1. The goal is to make this
ratio as small as possible (a value strictly below 1 would be a counterexample).
The constant graphon W == 0.5 attains the ratio exactly 1 and is used as the seed.

Returns:
    M: np.ndarray of shape (8, 8), symmetric, with all entries in [0, 1] -
        the step-graphon matrix.

szemeredi_trotter_incidences.docstring:
Szemeredi-Trotter incidence maximization. Construct a set of n points and a set of
m lines in the plane (on the integer lattice) so as to maximize the number of
point-line incidences (pairs (p, l) with p lying on l). Here the instance is fixed
at n = 54 points and m = 27 lines.

Baseline: the classical Szemeredi-Trotter extremal grid construction with k = 3.
    Points:  {1,...,k} x {1,...,2*k^2}                          -> 2*k^3 = 54 points
    Lines :  y = a*x + b  for a in {1,...,k}, b in {1,...,k^2}  ->   k^3 = 27 lines
Each line y = a*x + b passes through exactly k of the grid points (one per column
x in {1,...,k}, since a*x + b stays within {1,...,2*k^2}), giving k^4 = 81 total
incidences. This matches the Szemeredi-Trotter bound n^(2/3) m^(2/3) up to a constant.

Lines are encoded in homogeneous form (A, B, C) meaning A*x + B*y + C = 0, so the
line y = a*x + b becomes (a, -1, b).

Returns:
    points: np.ndarray of shape (54, 2), integer (x, y) lattice coordinates.
    lines : np.ndarray of shape (27, 3), integer (A, B, C) with A*x + B*y + C = 0.

turan_hypergraph_tetrahedron.docstring:
Hypergraph Turan number of the tetrahedron. Construct a weighted, blow-up
3-uniform hypergraph pattern (vertex weights plus a multiset of size-3 edges)
that contains no copy of the tetrahedron K4^(3), so as to maximize the Turan
density lower bound C. The blow-up density of an edge multiset {a,b,c} over
the (sum-normalized) vertex weights w is:
    - 6 * w[a]*w[b]*w[c]            if a,b,c are all distinct,
    - 3 * w[dup]^2 * w[other]       if exactly two coordinates coincide,
    - w[a]^3                        if a == b == c,
and C is the sum of these contributions over all (distinct) edges.

Baseline: the classical 5/9 construction (Turan's conjectured optimum for
K4^(3)) on 3 weighted vertices.

Returns:
    weights: np.ndarray of shape (V,), non-negative vertex weights.
    edges: np.ndarray of shape (E, 3) of int vertex indices in [0, V-1];
        each row is a size-3 multiset (repeats allowed) of vertices.

name: Climate dynamics: partial-observation Lorenz-96 assimilation
description: Design an ensemble analysis update that reconstructs an evolving twenty-variable chaotic state from noisy observations of half its coordinates. The evaluator propagates the ensemble and compares each updated ensemble mean with independent high-accuracy reference trajectories.

sources.locator: Tomizawa and Sawada (2021), Combining ensemble Kalman filter and reservoir computing to predict spatiotemporal chaotic systems; Section 2.1 Eq. (1) Lorenz-96 dynamics and Section 2.2 ensemble data assimilation.

evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: analyze(ensemble, observations, observed_indices, observation_variance) -> updated ensemble with the same (16,20) shape. Lorenz-96 dx_i/dt=(x_(i+1)-x_(i-2))*x_(i-1)-x_i+F with periodic indices, nondimensional units. Evaluator propagates each member by RK4 at dt=0.01 for five steps between updates, then observes even-indexed states with independent N(0,0.49) noise. Three runs F=6,8,10, seeds=181,283,389; 40 updates each. Score is pooled analysis-mean RMSE against independent DOP853 truth over all states and cycles. Output must be finite and within [-100,100]. name: Cosmology: compact dark-energy growth approximation
description: Improve a six-coefficient growth-index formula for the linear growth rate and normalized growth factor in smooth CPL dark-energy cosmologies. A tightly integrated general-relativistic second-order ODE provides an independent numerical reference. The score is the worst relative error across both observables on disjoint public validation cosmologies, extending the constant-gamma seed within a fixed compact ansatz.

sources.locator: Linder and Cahn, Parameterized Beyond-Einstein Growth; equations 1-3 and 8: growth-index ansatz and GR growth equation; equations 14-15: constant growth-index approximation.
Linder, Exploring the Expansion History of the Universe; equations 6 and 7 and following density evolution define the CPL background.

requirements.hardware: CPU
requirements.datasets: None downloaded; mathematical constructions or locally generated synthetic instances.

evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: construct() -> real vector of six finite coefficients in [-10,10]. At scale factor a, q=1-Om(a), u=1+w0+wa*(1-a), gamma=c0+c1*q+c2*q^2+c3*u+c4*wa*a+c5*u*q, and f=Om(a)^gamma. Gamma must lie in [0.1,1.2] at all checked locations. The evaluator computes D(a)/D(1)=exp(-integral_ln(a)^0 f(exp(x)) dx). Minimize 100 times the maximum relative error of both f and normalized D over validation models and a values.

limitations: Local synthetic approximation task, not an observational discovery or reproduction of a paper's fitted coefficients.
Uses general relativity, flat space and smooth dark energy; excludes nonlinear structure, modified gravity, radiation and neutrino effects.
The numerical reference uses the explicitly specified finite matter-era boundary D(ai)=D_x(ai)=ai at ai=0.001; it is not a full Boltzmann cosmology solver.
Calibration and validation models are disjoint but public. Better scores establish accuracy only on this finite model set and do not resolve the dark-energy problem.

name: Biology: Single-cell batch integration: public scIB adaptation
description: Integrate measured count matrices across experimental batches while preserving cell-type neighborhoods and rare populations under a declared transductive protocol.

sources.locator: scIB Methods: joint evaluation of biological conservation and batch correction.
Official author implementation/data reference; evaluator and seed are independently written, not copied.
Original scIB pancreas h5ad; rawcounts and genuine technology/cell-type annotations. Pinned SHA256 in data/science/biology_expansion/sources.json.

requirements.hardware: CPU
requirements.datasets: Pinned measured source bundle B04.json plus SHA256 receipt; automatically prepared by scripts/prepare_biology_expansion.py.

evaluation.benchmark: Biology: Single-cell batch integration: public scIB adaptation
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

notes: Repository also contains later added tasks; these are not automatically attributed to this paper.
Full external evaluation requires up to 500 GB RAM for tabula_sapiens; approximate evaluation is explicitly not the reportable paper metric.
execution.interface: integrate(counts, batch_labels) -> finite cells x dimensions embedding, 1<=dimensions<=128. No cell-type labels supplied. Transductive evaluation. Local scIB-inspired score =0.6 cell-type-macro kNN purity +0.4 within-cell-type batch mixing. Rare-type purity diagnostic. This is an adapted public scIB protocol, not reproduction of Station private scores.

provenance.note: New local evaluator and seed based on cited source specifications; official data are reused.

limitations: Measured scIB human-pancreas study:1000 hash-selected cells and500variable genes from raw-count layer,9genuine technology batches. Transductive local metrics, no fullscIB/Station score reproduction or cross-study claim.
Canonical Station upgrade using an explicitly adapted public scIB-style60/40 score. Does not reproduce the private Station evaluator or complete scIB metric suite; no trajectory conservation claim.
Public source subsets are development-visible. Freeze candidates before evaluating on additional independently chosen studies/instances; trusted candidate execution is not a security sandbox.
Improving this benchmark is a scientific-method result; it does not alone establish a new biological discovery.

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Separate cell identity from experimental batch effects in single-cell expression measurements.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Reliable integration allows biological cell populations to be compared across studies without confusing technical differences with cell biology.

papers.title: Fast, sensitive, and accurate integration of single cell data with Harmony
papers.primary_goal: Integrate single-cell data while retaining biological cell-type structure and accounting for experimental differences.
papers.task_relation: Harmony directly addresses cross-batch cell-state integration, including pancreatic-islet studies. The local transductive pancreas task measures batch mixing and preservation of annotated neighborhoods; it does not independently discover or validate new cell types.

science_relevance.reason: Harmony is accepted for its domain-specific biological integration objective and applications; the scIB benchmark paper alone is insufficient.
